lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first open declaration that he loves her books and her.

lines.text: Mr. Horne never spoke it to my ears--(I never saw him face to face in my life, although we have corresponded for long and long), and he never wrote it to my eyes.
lines.note: He promises that spring will bring their first meeting.

lines.text: You wished all manner of good to me one day as the clock struck ten; yes, and I assure you I was better that day--and I must not forget to tell you so though it is so long since.
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls his clock-striking good wish and its effect on her.

lines.text: Don't you remember I told you, once on a time that you 'knew nothing of me'? whereat you demurred--but I meant what I said, and knew it was so.
lines.note: Robert calls back to his earlier claim that she knew nothing of him.

lines.text: And you are NOT, NOT my 'other friend,' any more than this head of mine is my other head, seeing that I have got a violin which has a head too!
lines.note: A private joke rejecting the idea that she is only his 'other friend'.

lines.text: Do you remember what you said to me of cabbages versus poems, in one of the first letters you ever wrote to me?--of selling cabbages and buying Punches?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls his early cabbage-versus-poem comparison.
The moment his love becomes openly declared and claimed.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's sweeping image of his life wound around hers.

lines.text: My love--no words could serve here, but there is life before us, and to the end of it the vibration now struck will extend--I will live and die with your beautiful ring, your beloved hair--comforting me, blessing me.
lines.note: His response to her gift of ring and hair, sealing their bond.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: He declares that, if marriage did not exist, he would invent it.

lines.text: Do you remember when you wrote first to me ‘May God bless you and me in that!’
lines.note: Elizabeth remembers his first blessing and how it reached her before they met.

lines.text: And therefore, because you are the best, only dearest!——Robert.
lines.note: Elizabeth finally speaks his name, Robert, as her own.

lines.text: We shall soon know—if you live, you will be mine, I must think—you have put these dear arms too surely round my neck to be disengaged now.
lines.note: Robert's assurance that her life and his are bound together.

lines.text: Is this my last letter to you, ever dearest?
lines.note: Elizabeth's last letter, asking whether it is her final one.
